eyebrow: Dawn & twilight · the light that arrives before the Sun does
h1: The sky is lit for an hour before sunrise — and on a plane there is nothing above you for the Sun to light
tw-k9: left: a cross-section through the observer and the Sun, at true scale
tw-k10: the last ray to graze the ground at the terminator, passing overhead at height h
tw-k11: everything under that ray is in the planet's own shadow
tw-k12: right: the same three ceilings on a plain height axis in kilometres
tw-fcap1: Why there is light overhead and none underfoot. Drawn at true scale with no exaggeration at all — none is needed, and the thinness of the lit shell is itself the finding. Note what the picture does not contain: any assumption about how bright the scattering is. The claim is only that a boundary exists and that its height is set by R.
tw-lead: Long before the Sun clears the horizon the sky is already bright, and long after it has gone the sky stays bright a while longer. That is not the question this tab asks. The question is sharper and much harder for a flat model to answer: why is it bright up there while it is dark down here?
tw-lead2: A lit sky over an unlit ground is an asymmetry, and an asymmetry needs an edge. An edge needs a shadow. A shadow needs a body big enough and round enough to cast one. On a plane the Sun is above the plane at every hour of the day and night, so there is nothing anywhere that can be in shade while the air above it is in sunlight.
tw-gloss1: When the Sun is θ below your horizon, the last ray that grazes the Earth's surface passes over your head at a height h. Below h you are in the planet's shadow; above h the air is still in full sunlight and scatters some of it down to you. That single line is the whole of twilight, and it contains R — so twilight is a measurement of the radius, not merely a consequence of it. Put θ = 6°, 12° and 18° into it and out come 35 km, 142 km and 328 km, which is the table further down.
tw-h1: Three twilights, and why they stop where they stop
tw-p1: The three stages are defined by the Sun's geometric depression and by nothing else: civil twilight runs from sunset to 6° below, nautical from 6° to 12°, astronomical from 12° to 18°.[1]
tw-p1b: The names record what a person could still do. Through civil twilight you can carry on outdoors without a lamp and the horizon stays crisp. Through nautical twilight the sea horizon is still visible while the brighter stars are out, which is exactly the window in which a sextant sight works and is why sailors named it. By the end of astronomical twilight the sky no longer adds measurable light to a telescope's field.
tw-p2: Those are human conventions, chosen for human tasks. What is not a convention is the height each one corresponds to. The formula above turns each threshold into a height above your head, and the answers land on the structure of the atmosphere without having been aimed at it. The table computes them; nothing in it is typed in by hand.
tw-cap1: Each twilight threshold, turned into the height of the shadow's ceiling over the observer — computed from h = R(sec θ − 1) with R = 6,371 km
tw-th4: h as a fraction of R
tw-th5: What is still in sunlight up there
tw-call1: How much of that is an argument, and how much is a coincidence. Be careful here, because the temptation is to claim more than the geometry gives. The 6/12/18 thresholds were fixed by what people can do, not derived from air density, so the correspondence in the last column is a consistency check, not a derivation. What the geometry does give, with no wiggle room, is the mapping itself: an 18° Sun puts the shadow ceiling at 328 km and a 6° Sun puts it at 35 km, and those follow from R alone. The interesting part is that the point where a human stops being able to see the sky glow lands where the air runs out — and that the same R which fixes the horizon in the dip tab, the star altitudes in the navigation tab and the arrival times in the seismology tab also fixes this.
tw-h2: What the inverse-square law actually predicts on a plane
tw-p3: Now the flat model, taken seriously and given its best case. Put a Sun at height H above an infinite plane, let it be as small and as close as you like, and let its light fall off as the inverse square of distance — which is the correct law for a compact source and is the law flat-earth accounts appeal to when they explain sunset as the Sun becoming distant and dim. An observer at ground distance d from the point directly under it is at slant range r = √(H² + d²), and the light lands on the ground obliquely, at an angle whose cosine is H/r.
tw-gloss2: E is the illuminance on level ground — the quantity a light meter pointed at the sky measures, and the quantity the published twilight measurements report. ϑ is the Sun's apparent diameter, with D its real diameter. Both are elementary and both hold on a plane for any H, any D and any brightness I.
tw-p4: Divide each by its value at noon, when the observer stands directly under the Sun, and something useful happens: every free parameter cancels. H disappears. D disappears. The Sun's brightness disappears. What is left is a relation between two things you can measure with a phone.
tw-gloss3: On a plane, the ground can only get dark to the exact extent that the Sun gets small. Dim it by a thousand and it must have shrunk tenfold. That is not a claim about any particular flat map, or any particular Sun height, or any particular disc diameter — it is inverse-square geometry with the nuisance parameters divided out, in the same way the reciprocal zenith angles in the elevation tab cancel the two station heights. If you prefer the illuminance measured face-on to the rays rather than on level ground, drop the obliquity factor and the exponent becomes 2 instead of 3. It changes none of what follows.
tw-p5: So the flat model owes two numbers that must agree, and both have been measured to death. The measured day-to-night ratio of downwelling light is about one hundred million: a recent open-data study spanned it with two spectrometers precisely because no single instrument covers a factor of 108.[2] Full sun is of order 100,000 lux; a clear moonless night sky is of order 0.001 lux.[2][10]
tw-p5b: And the Sun's apparent diameter runs between 31.6′ and 32.7′ over a whole year, a 3% swing caused by the Earth's orbital eccentricity, and is constant to far better than a percent across any one day.[7]
tw-cap2: The flat model's own arithmetic, with the Sun at three heights that have been proposed — all computed, none fitted
tw-call2: The steel-man, and why it eats itself. H is the flat model's free parameter, so tune it in the flat model's favour: pick whatever H makes the night as dark as the night actually is. The answer is H ≈ 43 km on a 20,000 km disc — the Sun would have to be lower than a weather balloon's ceiling. But the relation above is a package deal. Buying a factor of 108 in brightness means buying a factor of 464 in apparent size, so that Sun would cross the sky shrinking from 32′ at noon to 4″ at midnight, from a disc to a star. Nobody has ever recorded that, and a mobile phone with a solar filter rules it out in an afternoon.
tw-call2b: Tune it back the other way, and it eats itself. Push H back up to keep the disc the right size and the night gets bright again: at the usual 5,000 km the model's midnight is one seventieth of noon, about the difference between direct sun and a dull overcast afternoon, not the difference between noon and starlight. There is no H that does both jobs, because the exponent linking them is fixed by geometry.
tw-k13: the inverse-square prediction for three Sun heights, out to the rim of the usual flat map
tw-k14: the measured night level, eight decades down[2]
tw-fcap2: Eight orders of magnitude, and where the flat curves stop. The vertical axis is the light on level ground relative to noon, on a log scale, so each gridline is a factor of ten; the horizontal axis is ground distance.
tw-p-gap: The gap is not a discrepancy that better numbers might close. The flat curves flatten out because a source at finite height never gets far away compared with itself, while the measurement falls off a cliff. On a globe there is no curve to draw at all past the terminator — the direct beam is geometrically zero there, and every photon that reaches you has been scattered down out of the sunlit shell above.
tw-h6: The two models side by side, in motion
tw-p14: Everything above compares one place at one moment. This panel puts the whole planet under both models at the same instant, because the disagreement is not really about how bright the sky is — it is about the shape of the lit region, and shape is the thing you can check without owning a light meter. On the left, a globe shaded by the Sun's altitude, with the three twilight thresholds drawn as the small circles they actually are. On the right, the same instant on the standard flat map, in two versions.
tw-p15: The second of those versions is the one that matters, and it is worth being clear about why it is not a straw man. Suppose everything is granted: forget the inverse square, forget the Sun's height, and assume only that brightness on a plane is some decreasing function of your distance from the point beneath the Sun. What that function is does not matter. Because it decreases, its contours are circles centred on the subsolar point — for every such function, without exception.
tw-p15s: So a flat Earth is committed to a circular day–night boundary whatever its photometry turns out to be, and the single remaining number, the radius, is then tuned in the flat model's favour: each ring is pinned so that the plane is exactly right at 45° N at that instant. It touches the truth at one latitude, by construction, and misses everywhere else. The dashed teal curve is where sunset is really happening, which is not a claim of this page but the content of the sunrise and sunset tables printed for every city on Earth.
tw-k1: the real day–night edge at that moment, from published rise and set tables
tw-k2: its ticks point into the night side
tw-k3: that morning's sunrise at 45° N, where the flat model is made correct
tw-k4: that evening's sunset at 45° N, the second calibration point
tw-fcap5: One instant, two geometries. The teal curve is not this page's assertion: it is the published rise and set tables, drawn as a line. One calibration pins both amber dots and every ring passes through them, so the plane is exact there by construction — the comparison is everywhere else. The globe's zone boundaries are computed, not traced; its daylight ramp is Lambert's cosine, but the ramp through twilight is interpolated, and schematic, because this page owns no scattering model.
tw-p15b: Watch the ticks reverse. In July the day–night curve hugs the lit region and they face outwards; in December it closes around the pole and they face in, because in December the pole is the part in darkness. That reversal is not a drawing choice — it is what a tilted planet does.
tw-p15c: The two halves do not animate alike, and it is worth knowing which. On the globe the viewpoint is fixed relative to the Sun, so the terminator holds still and the coastlines slide through it. On the flat map the coastlines are held still, in the orientation flat maps are always drawn in, and the lit patch sweeps across them instead. Both show the same rotation; they differ only in what they nail down. The right-hand panel offers two shadings: 1/r² shades the plane by E/E₀ = (H/r)³ with the Sun 5,000 km up, and Fitted instead draws the circular contours that any decreasing law is forced to produce.
tw-p17: Switch the right-hand panel to 1/r² and an obvious question arises: if the plane never goes dark on this map, then where does it go dark? The formula answers it. Solving E(d)/E(0) = 10−8 for the distance, with the Sun 5,000 km up, puts real night 2,320,800 km from the point beneath it — a hundred and sixteen times the radius of the whole flat map, and six times the distance to the Moon.
tw-p17s: Even a mere thousandfold dimming, which is still a bright overcast afternoon rather than night, does not arrive until 49,700 km, two and a half times the rim. Lowering the Sun does not rescue this: at 1,000 km, about the lowest anyone has proposed, night still needs 464,000 km, twenty-three times the map. The plane is simply too small for its own light to fall off across it, and that is not a defect of one flat map but of the inverse-square law applied to a source hanging a few thousand kilometres above a surface you can walk on.
tw-call4: The day almost nobody is in the dark. Set the panel to 8 July, 11:15 UTC and look at where the night is. Combining their solar data with a gridded population dataset, timeanddate found that at that moment it is night for just under 80 million people — so roughly 99% of humanity is receiving some sunlight at once, about 83% in full daylight and 16% somewhere in twilight.[11]
tw-call4b: What that number does and does not say. They are careful, and so is this page: around 3% of that total, some 257 million people, are in astronomical twilight, which is not distinguishable from night by eye, so the honest figure for perceptible light is nearer 96%.[11] It is also not unique to one date — it holds on about sixty days around the June solstice, with the daily peak falling between 11:00 and 11:03 UTC.[12] This page ships no population grid and does not recompute those percentages; it quotes them, and they are checkable against the sources.
tw-p16: Why is that an argument rather than a curiosity? Because the number is a census of who is standing inside the shadow, and the shadow's shape is precisely what the two models disagree about.
tw-p16s: It comes out that high because the middle of the night, on that date at that hour, sits in the emptiest part of the Pacific, while the tilt keeps the whole northern half of the planet — where most of humanity lives — in daylight at the same time. That is not a coincidence anybody arranged; it falls out of a tilted sphere turning once a day, and you can watch it fall out by pressing play.
tw-p16t: Then switch the right-hand panel between its two versions and ask which landmasses each one puts in the dark. They are not the same landmasses, and only one of the two answers agrees with the sunrise and sunset times published for those cities on that date.
tw-h3: The duration of twilight is the test with no radius in it
tw-p6: Everything so far has used R. This section does not, and that makes it the counterpart on this tab of the magnetism tab's dip law: a constraint on shape that survives any rescaling. Twilight lasts as long as the Sun takes to travel from the horizon down to 18° below it, and how long that takes depends on the angle at which the Sun's daily circle meets your horizon. At the equator it comes down almost vertically and the whole business is over in a little over an hour. At 50° north it slants, and in June it slants so much that the Sun never gets 18° down at all.
tw-gloss4: The first line is the hour angle at which the Sun stands at altitude h, for latitude φ and declination δ; the duration of a stage is the difference of two hour angles divided by 15.041° per hour. The second line is the Sun's altitude at local midnight, and it is the one that decides everything: if h_min never reaches −18°, there is no astronomical night at that place on that date, however long you wait. Notice that neither line contains R, or any distance at all, and an independent implementation of the same formulae is published by a different institution in a different country's service.[9] These are statements about a sphere's shape and its tilt, and they would read the same for a planet twice the size.
tw-p7: Set h_min = −18° and the condition falls out: astronomical night disappears above latitude 90° − 18° − δ. At the June solstice, with δ = 23.44°, that is 48.6°. Nautical night goes at 54.6° and civil night — the genuine white nights — at 60.6°. Those are three sharp latitudes, predicted from the obliquity of the ecliptic and nothing else, and every one of them can be checked by looking up a published almanac[8] or by going outside in June.
tw-p7c: Paris sits at 48.86°, a fifth of a degree past the first threshold, which is why Paris has no astronomical night for about two months either side of midsummer and Nice, 5° further south, has one every night of the year.
tw-cap3: Length of each twilight stage, computed from latitude and declination alone — sunrise taken at the standard −0°50′ for the centre of the disc
tw-k5: three solid curves: minutes from sunset to the end of civil, nautical and astronomical twilight
tw-k6: a vertical dashed line in each curve's colour: the latitude past which that stage never ends
tw-k7: the same journey to −18° at the equinox, which never blows up
tw-k8: each place sits on the deepest stage it still completes; a hollow ring completes none
tw-fcap3: Twilight length against latitude, and the three places it becomes infinite. All three curves are at midsummer — June in the north, December in the south — so the axis is latitude without a sign and Ushuaia is plotted at its own midsummer rather than pretended to be northern. The three latitudes are 48.6° for astronomical, 54.6° for nautical, 60.6° for civil.
tw-p7b: A flat model has no counterpart for any of this. Its Sun is above the plane at every instant, it never crosses a horizon, and nothing in an inverse-square falloff produces a latitude past which a stage takes infinitely long in June and eighty minutes in December.
tw-call3: This is a sign test, not a near miss. The page prefers these wherever it can get them, for the reason set out in the elevation tab: a disagreement of a few percent can always be blamed on the instrument, but a question with a yes and a no cannot. Does astronomical night occur at your latitude in the third week of June? At 48° the answer is yes and at 49° it is no, and the almanac agreed with the calculation for a century before anyone thought to argue about it. The flat model does not give a different answer here. It gives no answer, because it has no quantity whose sign could flip.
tw-h4: The Earth's shadow is an object, and you can photograph it
tw-p8: On a clear evening, turn your back on the sunset and look east about ten minutes after the Sun has gone. There is a dark blue-grey band lying along the horizon, with a soft pink band above it, and the boundary between them is straight enough to measure and slightly curved if you take in enough sky. The pink is sunlight reddened by its long passage through the lower atmosphere and back-scattered towards you — it has been called the Belt of Venus for a long time. The dark band under it is the Earth's own shadow, projected onto the air, seen edge-on.[6]
tw-p9: It behaves exactly as a shadow should. It appears opposite the Sun, centred on the antisolar point to within the accuracy anyone can hold a camera. Its top rises as the Sun sinks, at the Sun's own rate, so that its elevation above the eastern horizon tracks the Sun's depression below the western one. It is wider than the Sun because the Sun is not a point. And it fades out as it climbs, for the plainest of reasons: it is being projected onto air that is thinning as it goes up, so by the time the shadow's edge is 20° high there is nothing left up there to catch it.
tw-fcap4: The eastern sky at three moments after sunset. The dark segment is the geometric shadow of the Earth, drawn at the elevation the Sun's depression puts it, with the reddened band immediately above it. This is a schematic: the colours are indicative and the fading is drawn, not computed from a scattering model. What is computed is the height of the boundary in each frame, and that is the whole falsifiable content — an edge exists, it sits opposite the Sun, and its elevation equals the Sun's depression. The flat model predicts no edge at all in the eastern sky, because there is no body between the observer and the Sun to cast one and the Sun is never below the plane.
tw-h5: Four objections, and what each one costs
tw-refr: Refraction is real and this page models it everywhere, so before the objections, here is its size: at the horizon it lifts an object by about 34′, a little over half a degree, and that is the reason sunrise is reckoned with the Sun's centre at −0°50′ rather than at zero.
tw-p10-q: 1. "It is just perspective — the Sun goes too far away to see."
tw-p10: Perspective moves things towards a vanishing point; it does not switch them off, and it certainly does not switch off the ground while leaving the sky lit. If the Sun were merely far, its light would still be falling on your street at the same fraction of noon as on the air 200 km above your street, because both are essentially the same distance from it. The asymmetry is the whole phenomenon and perspective has nothing to say about it. Perspective also cannot make an edge: the shadow in the eastern sky has a boundary you can put a protractor on.
tw-p11-q: 2. "The Sun is a spotlight and its beam has a limited reach."
tw-p11: This is the stronger version, and it is worth taking seriously because it does at least produce a boundary. But it produces the wrong one. A spotlight on a plane illuminates a circle, and the edge of that circle is at a fixed distance from the sub-solar point, so the time your location spends in the fade is set by how fast that edge sweeps past — which is nearly the same everywhere and in every season. The measured twilight lasts 68 minutes at the equator, 107 minutes at Paris in March and never ends at Paris in June. A beam of fixed reach cannot do that. It also cannot put the fade boundary in the sky opposite the Sun rather than in the direction the beam is going.
tw-p12: Its size is priced above: about 34′ at the horizon, against the 1,080′ that twilight runs to — thirty times larger, and refraction shrinks rapidly as you move away from the horizon. There is also no free parameter left to spend: the refraction tab prices the flat limit k = 1 at a sustained inversion of +12.9 °C per 100 m, and radiosondes have been failing to find one since 1905.
tw-p13-q: 4. "The air simply gets dimmer as the light travels further through it."
tw-p13: Extinction along a long slant path is real too, and it is why the setting Sun is red and dim enough to look at. But extinction is a smooth, monotonic, exponential attenuation with air mass. It gives no threshold, no edge, and no dependence on the direction you look — whereas the observed twilight sky is bright in the west and dark in the east by an amount that tracks a single angle. And extinction cannot produce the latitude thresholds of the previous section, because the air mass along the path is a function of the Sun's altitude, and the whole point of that section is that the Sun's altitude at midnight is fixed by φ and δ in a way no atmospheric effect can touch.
tw-expt: Time first light against the clock, twice a year, from your own doorstep
tw-explead: This one costs nothing and needs no instrument beyond a phone and a clear horizon. Pick a spot with an open view east, go out well before sunrise on a clear morning near an equinox, and write down the clock time at which you can first make out the horizon line and the time the Sun's upper edge appears. Then do it again within a few days of the June solstice from the same spot. The interval is civil dawn, and the calculator below predicts both lengths from your latitude and the date alone, with no fitting and no free parameter. If you are north of about 48.6°, the more dramatic version is available to you: on the June nights the sky never goes properly dark at all, and the almanac will print a dash where the end of astronomical twilight should be.
tw-expiv:
Independent variable
What you change: the date, and therefore the Sun's declination. Two dates two months apart are enough at mid-latitudes; equinox against solstice is the sharpest pair. Changing your latitude instead works just as well if you are travelling.
tw-expdv:
Dependent variable
What you measure: the number of minutes between first light and sunrise. A clock and your own eyes. No angles, no instruments, no trust in anyone else's data.
tw-expmeta:
Hold constant: the site, the direction you face, and the criterion you use for "first light" — pick one and stick to it, because the criterion is worth several minutes and the effect you are after is tens of minutes. Clear sky both times; cloud on one morning and not the other ruins the comparison.
Kit: a phone. If you want the version with a number in it rather than a judgement call, point the phone's camera east on a tripod, shoot at fixed exposure every thirty seconds, and read the frame brightness afterwards — the curve is the twilight curve and its knee is unmistakable.
The tell: at 45° north the interval grows by roughly a quarter between March and June; at the equator it barely moves at all; north of 48.6° astronomical night vanishes outright in June. A flat Sun that dims by distance has no mechanism that makes the fade take longer in one month than another at the same place.
tw2-h2: How high the shadow stands — and why it climbs faster than the Sun sinks
tw2-p1: The table above gives the shadow's ceiling over your head, in kilometres. What you actually look at in the east is an angle, and the two are not the same number. Getting from one to the other takes no new physics, only the same formula applied twice. A patch of air lying angular distance ψ from you towards the antisolar point has the Sun that much further below its own horizon, at depression θ + ψ, so it is lit only if it clears its own ceiling: R(sec(θ + ψ) − 1). Follow a line of sight leaving your eye at altitude a, ask where along it that condition is first met, and the trigonometry collapses to one line.
tw2-call1: Sunlit at distance s along a sight line at altitude a, when the Sun is θ below the horizon: s · sin(a − θ) > R (1 − cos θ). Two consequences arrive with no free parameter whatever. First, if a ≤ θ the left-hand side is never positive, however far you look — so the top of the shadow always stands higher than the antisolar point, at every depression, above any atmosphere, on any sphere. It cannot be at or below it. Second, the whole sky goes shadowed once the ceiling rises past the layer that does the scattering, that is at cos θz = 1 / (1 + H/R) — which is the ceiling formula read backwards.
tw2-p2: Only one quantity there has to be supplied from outside: H, the effective top of the scattering layer, which is not a sharp surface — air density falls off smoothly, so the shadow's edge is a gradient rather than a line. Rather than pick a value, the table prints three and lets you see how little the interesting behaviour depends on the choice. What does not depend on it at all is the shape: the shadow rises faster than the Sun sinks, the ratio grows without bound, and the sky is fully shadowed at a depression of a very few degrees.
tw2-cap: Altitude of the top of the dark segment in the east, computed from s · sin(a − θ) = R(1 − cos θ) with R = 6,371 km — three values of the scattering-layer top H, none of them fitted to anything
tw2-foot: Depression at which the shadow reaches the zenith and the dark segment covers the sky: . Note what that means for an observer: the angle is the same everywhere on Earth, in every season — but the clock time it takes to get there is not, and runs from about thirteen minutes near the equator to three quarters of an hour at high latitude in spring.
tw2-exph: Experiment 1f-b · time the Earth's own shadow
tw2-expt: Turn your back on the sunset and photograph the east — a phone, a wall to rest it on, twenty minutes
tw2-explead: Ten minutes after sunset there is a dark blue-grey band along the eastern horizon with a pink one above it: the planet's own shadow, cast on its own air, with the Belt of Venus along its top edge.[6] Rest a phone on a wall, frame the eastern horizon with something vertical of known height in shot — a lamp post, a door frame, a distant mast — and shoot one fixed-exposure frame every minute from sunset until the band has climbed out of frame. Afterwards, convert the band's top edge into an angle using the object of known height and its distance. You will have the shadow's altitude against the clock, and the clock converts to the Sun's depression.
tw2-expiv:
Independent variable
What you change: the time since sunset, and therefore the Sun's depression θ, which an almanac gives you for your position to the minute.[1] Nothing else moves. If you can repeat it from a very different latitude, or six months later, do — that is where the sharper version lives.
tw2-expdv:
Dependent variable
What you measure: the altitude of the shadow's upper edge, in degrees, frame by frame. One angle per photograph, read off against a foreground object whose height and distance you know.
tw2-expmeta:
Hold constant: the camera position, the focal length and the exposure — an automatic exposure will chase the fading sky and move the very edge you are trying to follow. Pick one criterion for the top edge, the colour boundary rather than the brightness one, and keep it. Face the antisolar azimuth, not simply east: ten minutes after sunset the two differ by several degrees.
Kit: a phone, a wall, and a foreground object. If you want the angle without trigonometry, hold a ruler at arm's length — a centimetre at 57 cm subtends one degree, near enough for a two-degree effect.
The tells, stated in advance: the shadow's top is never below the antisolar point, at any moment, which the derivation above gives with no adjustable quantity; it accelerates, the ratio in the last column growing from about 1.1 to beyond 5 within twenty minutes; and the sky is fully shadowed at a depression of three to four and a half degrees — the same angle in Quito and in Reykjavík, though one takes a quarter of the time the other does.
tw2-expverd:
What this experiment cannot do, said plainly. It does not measure R. The single free quantity H is degenerate with the radius here — a bigger planet with a shallower atmosphere gives a similar curve — so anyone claiming a radius from a sunset photograph is claiming too much, and this page will not. Nor is the top edge sharp: air thins gradually, so two careful observers will disagree by something like half a degree, which is a few kilometres of H. What the experiment does settle is shape, and shape is what the two models disagree about.
The verdict rule, symmetric. The sphere fails if the shadow's top is ever measured at or below the antisolar point, if it climbs at a constant ratio rather than an accelerating one, or if the depression at which it reaches the zenith turns out to depend on where you stand or on the season. The flat model fails if a boundary it must explain as distance and haze instead behaves as a shadow does: an arc curved about the antisolar point, rising at an accelerating angular rate, closing over the sky at one fixed solar depression that is the same for every observer on the planet while the clock time is not.
tw-n1: Caveats this page owes you. Four, and the first is the one that matters. The heights in the first table are the geometric ceiling of the shadow; they are not a brightness model. Real twilight brightness involves multiple scattering, ozone absorption in the Chappuis band and aerosol loading, and the classical treatments are Hulburt's and Rozenberg's, not a one-line formula.[3][4][5] Second, the durations here use the mean Sun and a spherical Earth, with sunrise at the conventional −0°50′; published almanacs will differ from them by a minute or two, and a mountain horizon by rather more. Third, the measured 108 day-to-night ratio is downwelling irradiance at one dark rural site, and the same study measures a factor of 100 between that site and a city — the number is a scale, not a constant. Fourth, the anti-twilight figure is a schematic, and its colours are drawn rather than computed. None of the four moves an argument that turns on eight orders of magnitude against fewer than two, and on a stage length that goes to infinity at a latitude you can point to on a map.
tw-n2: The through-line. The dip tab measures how far the horizon falls below level; this tab measures how far the shadow rises above it, which is the same geometry read upwards instead of downwards, and it arrives at the same R. Then the duration section drops R entirely and constrains the shape on its own, the way the magnetism tab does. And the inverse-square section is the page's method in miniature: take the flat model's own physics, divide out its free parameters until nothing adjustable is left, and see what it is then obliged to predict. Here it is obliged to predict that the night is seventy times darker than the day. Go outside and see whether it is.
rd-note: Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.
layer-ground: nothing: the ceiling is at your feet. This is sunset.
layer-strato: mid-stratosphere, above the ozone peak — about 99% of the atmosphere's mass is already below it
layer-thermo: thermosphere — the height auroras are seen at, and where meteors burn up
layer-iss: the altitude the space station orbits at — there is essentially nothing left up there to scatter light
matches: matches — at the cost of the disc
geom-reads-tpl: Ceiling of the Earth's shadow over your head, from h = R(sec θ − 1) with R = {R} km: {h6} km at 6° · {h12} km at 12° · {h18} km at 18°. The left panel is at true scale, which is why the 6° shell is barely a line — that thinness is the point, not a drawing fault.
world-reads-head-tpl: Day {N} of the year, {utc}. Sun overhead at {sub}; the middle of the night is at {anti}.
world-reads-inv-tpl: Plane shaded by E/E₀ = (H/r)³, H = {H} km. It never reaches night anywhere on the map: the dimmest point, out at the {rim} km rim, is 1/{dim} of noon. For a real night — 1/100,000,000 — you would have to be {dNight} km from the point under the Sun, which is {xMap}× the whole map and {xMoon}× the distance to the Moon.
world-reads-fit-tpl: Dashed teal = the real day–night edge at this instant, the line the published sunrise and sunset tables trace out. Its short ticks point into the night side, so the loop encloses the night rather than the day — worth checking at the December preset, where it closes around the pole. Hollow dot = that morning's sunrise at {cal}° N, solid dot = that evening's sunset. Both sit at the same map distance from the Sun, so one calibration pins the rings through both; any decreasing law gives rings, so only their radii were free and they have been spent there.
exp-out-tpl:
Civil {c}  ·  Nautical {n}  ·  Astronomical {a}
Total sunset → −18°: {t}. Sun's altitude at local midnight: {m}°.
Astronomical night vanishes above latitude {thr18}° · nautical above {thr12}° · civil above {thr6}°.
exp-verd-all-tpl: Verdict rule. At {phi}° with the Sun at {dec}°, the globe says there is no astronomical night at all on this date, because the Sun bottoms out at {m}° and never reaches −18°. Look up the almanac for these coordinates: it should print a dash. If it prints a time — if the sky does go fully dark here on this date — the geometry on this tab is wrong and you should say so.
exp-verd-tpl: Verdict rule. The globe predicts {t} from sunset to full dark, and predicts it from your latitude and the date alone. Time it. If your measured civil dawn is within a few minutes of {c}, the prediction stands; if it is out by a quarter of an hour on a clear morning with a flat horizon, something here is wrong. And the sharper test is free: move {dlat}° of latitude towards the pole and astronomical night should disappear entirely on this date.
